Foundations: Choosing Your Product's Approval Route

Before you fill any form, you need to know which NAFDAC route your product fits, what must be ready before you apply, and who in your business owns compliance. This module turns those three questions into decisions you can write down.
Micro scale, small scale or full registration: finding your product's NAFDAC route
Check whether your product is allowed under NAFDAC's micro and small scale scheme
Decide between the micro scale and small scale routes using staff, premises and product count
Choose which products to list first when you make more than five
Explain what a listing certificate is and how long it lasts

You already know that a packaged food or cosmetic needs NAFDAC approval before it is sold to the public. This lesson goes one level deeper: **which door do you knock on?** NAFDAC runs a special scheme for micro and small enterprises (MSMEs), with lower fees, simpler documents and an inspection you can book on a date that suits you. Many hands-on makers qualify, but not every product and not every workshop does. Getting the route right first saves you from paying for the wrong application.
A woman worker in a small factory
Your route depends on what you make, how many people make it and where they work.
Which products the MSME scheme accepts

NAFDAC's MSME page lists the product types it accepts. On the food side it names bread, packaged water, and cottage or kitchen-scale and micro-scale foods. It also states that some foods are **not** allowed under the micro scale route: meat and meat products (except dried), milk and dairy products, and fish and fish products (except dried). These are higher-risk foods because germs grow in them quickly.

On the cosmetic and household side, the page lists petroleum jelly, shea butter, oil-based hair cream, oils such as coconut oil, laundry detergents, starch, liquid air freshener and soaps. It says complex cosmetics, pressurised sprays and hand sanitisers do not qualify. If your product is not on these lists, it goes through NAFDAC's regular registration route, which asks for more documentation.

Micro scale or small scale?

Inside the scheme there are two levels. NAFDAC describes a **micro scale facility** as a business with not more than five employees, in a building that can be purpose-built or adapted, with at least a **designated standard room that does not open directly to any source of contamination** (for example a toilet, a refuse dump or an open gutter). A **small scale facility** must have adequate space, capacity and equipment, and it is asked for more paperwork: written standard operating procedures (SOPs) for production, cleaning, hygiene, quality assurance and distribution, water analysis, and certificates of analysis for raw materials and finished products.

Two more rules shape your choice. Under micro scale, **not more than five products** can be registered. And what you receive at micro scale is a **listing certificate**, which NAFDAC states is valid for **two years**. Mark that date the day you collect it, because selling after expiry puts you back where you started.

If you answer no at any step, look at small scale or full registration instead.
Worked example: seven products, five slots

For example, Amaka in Enugu has three workers and a spare room she has converted for production. She makes seven products: chin-chin, coconut candy, plantain chips, zobo concentrate, whipped shea butter, black soap and a liquid laundry detergent.
She checks each product type against the MSME lists. All seven appear to fit allowed categories, so none is excluded by type.
She has three workers, within the five-employee limit for micro scale, and a dedicated room with no direct opening to a toilet or drain.

Seven products is more than the five allowed at micro scale, so she ranks them by monthly sales: chin-chin 300 packs, shea butter 120 jars, plantain chips 110 packs, black soap 90 bars, detergent 60 bottles, coconut candy 40 packs, zobo 25 bottles.
She lists the top five first. Together they are 680 of her 745 monthly units.
She works out the share: 680 divided by 745 is about 0.91, so 91 percent of her volume will be covered by the first applications.

Amaka applies at micro scale for five products covering about 91 percent of her sales, and pauses coconut candy and zobo for public sale until she can add them, possibly by moving up to small scale later.
A route is about the facility too

The same shea butter can qualify in one woman's workshop and fail in another's. If your only production space is the family kitchen that also opens onto the toilet passage, fix the room first. The route depends on where and how you make the product, not only on what it is.
When to go straight to small scale
You already employ more than five people in production, so you are beyond NAFDAC's micro scale facility description.
You want to list more than five products in the near future and do not want to apply twice.
You already work from a purpose-built space with enough room and equipment for larger batches.
You can write the SOPs (cleaning, hygiene, production, quality, distribution) and pay for water analysis and certificates of analysis.

Write your decision on one page: product names, the category each falls under, your staff count, a one-line description of your production room, and the route you have chosen. This page becomes the first sheet of your compliance file and the starting point for the rest of the course.

Building your vetting pack: locked formula, honest shelf life and a label that passes
Lock a written formula and process before you apply
Set a best-before date from your own storage checks instead of guessing
Prepare the vetting sample, three labels and the supporting certificates
Lay out every label field NAFDAC's MSME procedure asks for

NAFDAC's MSME procedure asks for a small set of items: evidence of CAC registration, a site use agreement where it applies, trademark documentation (optional at micro scale), **one vetting sample and three labels**, a fumigation certificate, food handler or medical fitness certificates for staff, and the payment receipt. Most delays come from the parts that only you can produce: a stable product and a correct label. This lesson is about those.
A woman holding a finished document beside a checklist
A complete vetting pack means the inspector sees a product that is already settled.
Step 1: lock the formula

The sample NAFDAC tests must be the product you will sell. If you change the recipe after approval, you are selling something that was not assessed. Before you apply, write a **master formula**: every ingredient, its supplier, the exact quantity per batch in grams or millilitres, and the method in numbered steps with times and temperatures. Make at least three batches from this sheet and check that they come out the same.
Worked example: turning a kitchen recipe into a master formula
For example, Rukayat in Ilorin makes whipped shea butter by feel: a scoop of shea, some coconut oil, a few drops of fragrance oil.
She weighs one normal batch: 1,600 g shea butter, 300 g coconut oil, 80 g sweet almond oil and 20 g fragrance oil. Total 2,000 g.
She converts to percentages: 1,600 divided by 2,000 is 80 percent shea; coconut 15 percent; almond 4 percent; fragrance 1 percent. The four add up to 100 percent.
She writes the method: melt shea and oils at low heat, cool until just setting, whip 8 minutes, fill 200 g jars.
From 2,000 g she fills 10 jars of 200 g each.
She makes three batches from the sheet. All three fill 10 jars, smell the same and set the same.
Rukayat now has a master formula she can scale (for 4,000 g, double every weight) and a product that is the same every time, which is what the vetting sample must represent.
Step 2: set an honest best-before date

Do not copy another brand's shelf life. Keep **retained samples** from each trial batch, sealed in the real pack, in the conditions a buyer would use: a shelf at room temperature, away from sun. Check them at fixed points, for example every two weeks, for smell, colour, texture, mould, rancidity or separation. Write each result down. Set your best-before date **shorter than the last check that was still fully good**. If you need longer life, a food or cosmetic testing laboratory can test for microbes and rancidity, and its report will strengthen your file.

Step 4: book the certificates that take time
**Fumigation certificate:** arrange pest control for the production premises by a pest control operator and keep the certificate.
**Medical fitness certificates:** NAFDAC lists sputum, stool, urine, Widal and Hepatitis B tests for food handlers. Book these for everyone who will touch the product.
**Site use agreement:** if you rent or use a relative's building, get a signed letter or tenancy showing you may use it for production.
**Trademark:** optional at micro scale, but start it if you plan to grow, because it protects your brand name.
Put all of these in one folder, paper or on your phone, and name each file clearly, for example '2026-03 fumigation certificate.pdf'. When the portal asks for uploads, you will not be searching.

Owning compliance as the producer: roles, touts and the real cost of shortcuts
Name a compliance lead and write clear duties for each person in production

A NAFDAC number is not a sticker you buy. It is a promise that a named business, in a named place, makes a product the same safe way every time. If something goes wrong, the name and address on your label lead back to you. That is why the business owner, not the cousin who helps or the agent who 'knows people', has to own compliance.
A small team working together around a shared plan

Give compliance a name and a desk
In a small workshop, the owner is usually the **compliance lead**. If you have staff, write down who does what. A short role sheet on the wall works better than instructions given once and forgotten.

Responsibility rests at the top, but daily habits at the base keep it real.

Responsibility also runs backwards to your suppliers. If you buy shea butter, palm kernel oil, flour or fragrance from a market trader, the trader's word is not proof of quality. Buy from sellers who give a receipt with their name, keep that receipt with the batch record, and check packed ingredients for a NAFDAC number and an expiry date. A cheap drum of oil with no label can ruin a batch, and the complaint will come to you, not to the trader.

Finally, give yourself one fixed hour each month as **compliance day**. Open the file, check that certificates are in date, read the last month of batch and cleaning records, and note anything to fix. Owners who protect that hour rarely get caught by surprise.
Shortcuts that cost more than they save
Pressure from buyers pushes some makers toward shortcuts. Here are the common ones, and why each one is dangerous for you and your customers.
**Borrowing another brand's number.** The number belongs to a different product and premises. If anything goes wrong, you have no defence.
**Inventing a number or printing 'NAFDAC approved'.** This is misleading and can lead to seizure of your stock and loss of the customers you worked hard to win.

**Paying someone who promises a number in a week.** NAFDAC's own procedure involves inspection and laboratory analysis, with a stated timeline of ninety working days. A promise that skips those steps is a warning sign.
**Approving one formula and selling another.** Swapping a cheaper oil or preservative after approval means the product on the shelf was never assessed.
How to protect yourself from agents

Apply through NAFDAC's e-registration portal (registration.nafdac.gov.ng) or a NAFDAC state office, and pay only against an official payment advice through Remita. Keep your own login. If someone asks for cash 'for the inspector', do not pay. NAFDAC lists 0800-1-NAFDAC (0800-1-623322) for complaints and 0700-1-NAFDAC for enquiries.
Worked example: a supermarket order and a tempting offer
For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes coconut candy. A supermarket wants 200 packs a month but needs a NAFDAC number. A man at the market offers to 'arrange' a number for her in seven days for a fee.
Funmi asks: will there be an inspection of my room and lab tests of my product? He says no. That alone tells her it is not a genuine registration.
She calculates what she risks: 200 packs at about ₦1,500 each (approximate) is ₦300,000 of monthly sales that could be seized, plus the supermarket relationship.
She tells the buyer honestly that her application is starting, and asks whether they can begin once her listing certificate arrives.
She submits on the portal, books her inspection for three weeks ahead, and sends the buyer a short update every month.
Funmi starts later than she hoped, but with a real number tied to her own premises, and a buyer who has seen her handle the process professionally.

We sell only products that match the approved formula and label.
We never print a number we were not issued, and never use another brand's number.
We record every batch and keep retained samples.
We stop selling a batch at once if there is a safety complaint, until we understand it.
We deal with NAFDAC directly, using our own login and official payments.
Print your non-negotiables and put them where your team works. When a busy week tempts someone to skip a step, the rule is already decided, so nobody has to argue about it.

Systems: The Application, the Production Room and the Numbers

This module takes you through the NAFDAC e-registration process and inspection day, shows you how to set up a production room that passes good manufacturing and hygiene checks, and teaches you to build compliance costs into your unit price and batch plan.
From portal to certificate: the application and inspection day, stage by stage
Move through the six stages of NAFDAC's MSME procedure in order
Convert ninety working days into a realistic calendar plan
Prepare your room, records and people for the inspector's visit
Respond correctly if the inspection or laboratory result is not satisfactory

NAFDAC's MSME procedure has six stages: apply online (or get forms at a state office), submit the completed form with documents, book your facility inspection, have samples collected during the inspection and sent to the laboratory, get scheduled for approval once the good manufacturing practice (GMP) inspection and lab results are satisfactory, and collect your certificate. The stated timeline from the first stage to the last is **ninety working days**. This lesson is about doing each stage well, so your file does not stall.
A person inspecting items with a magnifying glass
Inspection day is where your room, records and product are checked together.
Stages 1 and 2: the portal and the payment
Create your account on NAFDAC's e-registration portal (registration.nafdac.gov.ng) with your business email and a phone number you control. Write the login in your compliance file.
Enter your company details exactly as they appear on your CAC certificate. A different spelling or address causes queries.
Add each product with its name, pack size and category, using the same wording as your label.
Upload clear scans or photos of each document. One document per file, named clearly.
NAFDAC issues a payment advice. Pay through Remita using that advice only, and keep the receipt, which is itself one of the required documents.
Stage 3: booking the inspection

The procedure lets you **choose a convenient date** for the facility inspection. Use that freedom wisely. Pick a date at least two weeks after your fumigation, when your medical certificates are already in hand, and on a day you are actually producing, so the inspector can see your process, not an empty room.
A 90 working day plan
Week 1: apply and pay
Weeks 2 to 4: prepare room
Week 5: inspection and samples
Weeks 6 to 15: lab and review
Week 18: collect certificate
Ninety working days is about eighteen weeks, so plan around four months, not four weeks.
Worked example: planning around a trade fair
For example, Chiamaka in Aba wants her liquid laundry detergent approved before a trade fair in early October. It is now late April.
She converts the timeline: 90 working days divided by 5 working days a week is 18 weeks.
She adds two weeks of buffer for public holidays and queries, giving 20 weeks.
Counting 20 weeks from 1 May takes her to about mid-September.
She applies on 1 May, books fumigation for 6 May, staff medical tests for the same week, and picks an inspection date in the first week of June.
She sets a reminder to check the portal every Friday for queries.
Her plan finishes around mid-September with a few weeks to spare before the fair. If she had started in July, the timeline could not have fitted.
Stage 4: what the inspector looks at
The inspection checks good manufacturing practice and good hygiene practice. Prepare as if you were the inspector. Walk into your own room and look for the things below.
**The room:** a designated production room that does not open directly onto a toilet, refuse or drain; clean walls, floor and work surfaces; screened windows.
**Water:** a clean, reliable supply for production and handwashing, with soap and a clean towel or paper.
**People:** workers in clean aprons and hair covers, with their medical fitness certificates on file.
**Materials:** raw materials stored off the floor, labelled, with supplier receipts; finished goods kept apart.
**Records:** your master formula, batch records, cleaning log and fumigation certificate, ready to show.
**Product:** enough finished product from a normal batch for samples to be taken for the laboratory.
Keep a 'show file' on the table
Put every document the inspector may ask for in one folder in the order of the checklist above. Calm, quick answers show that your system is real.
Stages 5 and 6: results, queries and the certificate

Approval is scheduled only after satisfactory GMP and laboratory results. If the inspector notes problems, you may be asked to correct them. Treat every query as a task list: fix each item, take a dated photo or get a document as proof, and reply through the official channel. Do not argue, and do not change the product to pass a test unless you update the formula and label to match.

When you are notified, collect the certificate, then scan it and keep the original safe. Write the issue date and the expiry date (two years later for a micro scale listing) on the first page of your compliance file and in your phone calendar, with a reminder six months before expiry. Only now do you add the number to your label artwork and print stock.

Setting up a production room that passes GMP and hygiene checks
Arrange a room so materials move one way, from raw to finished
Set up handwashing, cleaning and pest control that an inspector can see working
Apply the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in a small production space
Write a daily cleaning log your team actually fills

NAFDAC's description of a micro scale facility asks for a **designated standard room that is not open directly to any source of contamination**. The word designated matters: it is a room used for production, not a family kitchen that also feeds the household, stores schoolbags and dries clothes. You do not need a factory. You need a clean, controlled room and habits that keep it that way.
A broom for cleaning
Cleaning that is scheduled and recorded is what makes a room inspection-ready.
One-way flow: raw in, finished out

Contamination happens when dirty and clean things cross. Arrange your room so that raw materials enter on one side, move through preparation and processing, and leave as packed product on the other side, without going backwards. Waste should leave by a route that does not pass the packing table.
Production room flow
Raw material store
Weighing and preparation
Processing or mixing
Cooling and filling
Labelling and packed storage
Materials move in one direction so finished product never meets raw or waste.
Worked example: converting a spare room
For example, Grace in Jos has a spare room about 3 metres by 4 metres for chin-chin production. Its back door opens toward the compound toilet.
She works out the floor area: 3 m times 4 m is 12 square metres, enough for one worktable, a gas burner area, a cooling rack and a packing table.
Because the back door faces the toilet, she seals it and uses only the front door, which opens to the corridor.
She places a raw material shelf by the door, mixing table next, the frying area under the window with a screened mesh, the cooling rack after it, and the packing table in the far corner.
She installs a handwashing point inside the door with a covered bucket and tap, liquid soap and paper towels.
She buys a pedal bin with a lid, puts shelves 15 cm off the floor, and paints the walls in washable paint.
Grace's room now matches a one-way flow, has no direct opening to the toilet, and has handwashing and storage an inspector can see.

Hygiene habits the inspector expects
**People:** clean apron, hair cover, short clean nails, no jewellery on hands, and nobody works on production while sick with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
**Pest control:** screened windows, no food left out overnight, sealed containers, and a fumigation certificate from a pest control operator. Never spray insecticide near open product or packaging.
**Cleaning:** a written schedule: surfaces after each batch, floor daily, shelves weekly, a deep clean monthly.
**Chemicals:** cleaning chemicals stored on a separate shelf, away from ingredients, in their original labelled containers.
**Packaging:** new containers stored covered and off the floor. Do not reuse old bottles from the market.
Gas, heat and cleaning chemicals

Keep gas cylinders outside or in a ventilated spot away from the frying area, with a working regulator and hose. Keep a fire blanket or extinguisher within reach. Never mix bleach with other cleaners, because some combinations release harmful gas.
Surfaces, equipment and storage

Inspectors look closely at anything that touches the product. Work tables should be smooth and easy to wash, such as stainless steel or a sealed surface; rough wood holds dirt and moisture. Use food-grade plastic or stainless steel bowls, spoons and buckets, and keep them only for production. A pot that cooks family soup at night should not mix shea butter in the morning. Store dry raw materials in sealed containers on shelves, label each one with what it is and the date it was opened, and use the oldest stock first. For cosmetics and soaps, keep fragrance oils and colourants tightly closed, away from heat and sunlight.

Lighting matters too. A dim room hides dirt and makes it hard to see a foreign object in the product. Add a bright bulb with a cover over the main work table, so a broken bulb cannot drop glass into an open batch.
Make cleaning visible with a log

A cleaning log is a simple table on the wall: date, task, done by, checked by. One line per day. It proves to the inspector, and to you, that cleaning really happens. Keep old sheets in your compliance file. A clean room with no record looks the same as a room cleaned once for the visit.

Pricing compliance into every unit and planning batch capacity
List every compliance cost for one product, one-off and recurring
Spread compliance costs over the units you will sell during the certificate's life
Plan batch sizes and production days that meet a buyer's monthly order
Check that the final unit price still leaves profit

Compliance is a real cost of production, like oil or packaging. If you do not build it into your price, it quietly eats your profit. The good news is that, once spread over hundreds of units, it usually adds only a small amount to each pack. This lesson shows you how to calculate it and how to plan capacity once bigger buyers start ordering.
An open ledger book
Compliance costs belong in your costing sheet like any other input.
Step 1: list your compliance costs

Separate costs that happen once per certificate from those that recur. For the NAFDAC fee, use the payment advice you receive. When this course was written, NAFDAC's MSME page showed the micro scale fee as ₦36,737.50 for food and ₦41,000 for cosmetics; fees can change, so always confirm on the page or advice. Other costs, such as medical tests or fumigation, vary by city and provider, so get quotes.

Step 2: spread the cost over units
Worked example: compliance cost per pack of chin-chin
For example, Grace in Jos uses the figures in the table above for her chin-chin. She sells about 300 packs a month and her micro scale listing lasts two years.
She plans to repeat fumigation and medical tests once in the second year as well, adding 25,000 + 45,000 = ₦70,000. Two-year total: ₦276,737.50.
Units sold over two years: 300 packs a month times 24 months = 7,200 packs.
Compliance cost per pack: 276,737.50 divided by 7,200 = about ₦38.44, which she rounds up to ₦40.
Her other costs per pack (ingredients, gas, packaging, labour) come to ₦620. Total cost is now ₦660.
At her selling price of ₦1,000, profit per pack is ₦340. Compliance takes ₦40 of each pack, which is affordable, and it unlocks supermarket sales she could not reach before.
If volume is low

If Grace sold only 50 packs a month, the same costs over 1,200 packs would be about ₦231 per pack. Low volume makes compliance expensive per unit, which is why the products you list first should be your best sellers.

Step 3: plan capacity for a bigger buyer

Once you have a number, a supermarket may ask for a fixed monthly quantity. Before you agree, check that your approved room and process can make it without cutting corners. Work in batches, because your batch record and batch number are tied to each one.
Write your batch size from the master formula, for example 60 packs per batch.
Write how many batches you can make safely in one production day, including cleaning between batches, for example 2.
Work out daily output: 60 times 2 = 120 packs.
Divide the monthly demand by daily output. For 300 existing packs plus a new 200-pack order, 500 divided by 120 is about 4.2, so 5 production days a month.
Check raw materials, packaging and cash for 5 days of production before you say yes.
Step 4: protect your cash between batches

Supermarkets and distributors often pay some weeks after delivery, while you pay for ingredients, packaging and gas before you produce. Ask each buyer for their payment terms in writing before the first delivery. Then work out how many weeks of production you must fund before the first payment arrives. For example, if one month of production for a new 200-pack order costs about ₦124,000 (200 packs at ₦620) and the buyer pays 30 days after delivery, you need at least that amount set aside, plus a cushion, before you accept. Do not take money meant for the next listing renewal or fumigation to fund a big order; keep a separate small savings pot for compliance so those dates are always covered.
Review your compliance cost per unit once a year. If sales grow, the cost per unit falls and you may be able to hold your price while competitors raise theirs.

If the numbers do not fit, say so and agree a smaller starting quantity. A buyer forgives a modest first order far more easily than a missed delivery or a batch made in a rush that fails quality checks.

Growth: Standards, Traceability and Staying Approved

Approval is the start, not the finish. This module covers SON's MANCAP certification for products outside NAFDAC's scope, the batch records and recall plan that protect you as you grow, and the renewal calendar and 90-day plan that keep your products legally on the shelf.
Selling wider: SON MANCAP, Nigerian Industrial Standards and buyer requirements
Explain what MANCAP is and which sectors SON lists under it
List the documents and steps SON gives for MANCAP certification
Prepare a supplier pack for a supermarket or distributor
Decide whether NAFDAC, SON or both apply by checking with the right office

Not every maker sells food or cosmetics. Women in Nigeria also produce adire and other textiles, leather bags and sandals, candles, simple electrical items, building materials such as paving stones and blocks, and more. For many locally manufactured products, the body that matters is the **Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON)**, through its **Mandatory Conformity Assessment Programme (MANCAP)**.
A person standing beside a large certificate with a seal
MANCAP certification shows a buyer your product meets a Nigerian Industrial Standard.
What MANCAP is

SON describes MANCAP as a product certification scheme for locally manufactured products in Nigeria, set up in 2006, to check that products comply with the relevant **Nigerian Industrial Standards (NIS)** before they are sold or exported. SON's service page lists six sectors: textiles and leather products; electrical and electronics; chemical products; mechanical products; civil, building and mining; and food products.
NAFDAC and SON: ask, do not assume

Food, drinks and cosmetics sold to the public need NAFDAC approval. SON's MANCAP sector list also includes food and chemical products, so for some products both bodies may have a role. Before you spend money, ask your nearest SON state office whether your product has an NIS and needs MANCAP, and keep their answer in writing.
MANCAP steps, from SON's own FAQ
Contact your nearest SON state office for the application form and guidance, or apply on the MANCAP platform (mancap.son.gov.ng).

Submit your CAC certificate, an on-the-spot test report from a SON laboratory or a laboratory accredited by the Institute of Public Analysts of Nigeria (IPAN), and proof of payment for the form and certification.
Prepare for factory inspections. SON states that at least two quarterly inspections take place before certification.
Receive the MANCAP certificate and the MANCAP logo, which carries a unique identification number. SON gives 60 days from receipt of a complete application.
Expect continued quarterly inspections while the certificate is valid. It is valid for three years, after which you recertify.

SON's FAQ also mentions a **six-month fast track verification** for MSMEs, which lets a small producer trade while working towards full certification, and states that MANCAP-certified products can be exported to West African countries. Fees vary, so SON directs applicants to its state offices for current charges.
The MANCAP cycle
Apply with test report
Two quarterly inspections
Certificate and logo
Quarterly surveillance
Recertify after three years
MANCAP is a three-year cycle with inspections throughout, not a one-time stamp.
Worked example: adire for a retail chain
For example, Bola in Abeokuta dyes adire fabric with four workers. A retail chain wants to stock her fabric, and a trader wants to take some to Accra.
Bola visits the SON state office and asks whether her fabric falls under a Nigerian Industrial Standard and needs MANCAP. She writes down the officer's name and answer.
She is told which tests apply, for example colour fastness, and arranges an on-the-spot test report at a SON or IPAN-accredited laboratory.
She plans for two quarterly inspections before certification, so she expects at least six months from her first inspection, and asks about the MSME fast track.
She builds a three-year calendar: certificate date, then a reminder every three months for surveillance inspections, and a recertification reminder six months before the third anniversary.
Bola knows her timeline before promising dates to the retail chain, and MANCAP certification will also support her export sales within West Africa.
Getting ready for SON's inspections

The habits from Module 2 carry over. SON inspectors want to see that you make the product the same way every time and can show it. Write down your raw material specifications (for example fabric type and dye brand for adire, or cement grade and mix ratio for paving stones), keep records of each production run, and keep your test reports filed by date. Because surveillance continues every quarter for three years, the records must stay alive, not be prepared once for the first visit. Use the MANCAP logo only on products and pack sizes covered by your certificate, since its unique number links the mark to your factory.

Batch records, traceability and recalls: training your team to keep them
Design a batch numbering system that links every pack to its production record
Fill in a batch manufacturing record and a distribution record
Handle a customer complaint and run a recall step by step
Train a new worker on records using a show, do, check method

As you grow, products leave your hands and travel to shops and homes you never see. **Traceability** means that from any one pack, you can find out when it was made, from which raw materials, by whom, and where the rest of that batch went. It is what lets you deal with a problem in one batch without losing your whole business.
A clipboard with a record sheet
Every batch gets a record, and every record can be traced to the packs on shelves.
A batch number that means something

A batch is everything made from one mix under the same conditions. Give each batch a unique code and print it on every pack from that batch. A simple pattern: **product code, date, batch of the day**. For example, CC-260312-02 means chin-chin, made on 12 March 2026, second batch that day. Anyone in your team can read it, and it never repeats.
The batch manufacturing record
Section
What to record
Header
Product, batch number, date, batch size, made by, checked by
Raw materials
Each ingredient, quantity used, supplier, supplier's batch or receipt date, expiry date
Process
Key times and temperatures, for example oil temperature and frying time; any problems
Yield
Units packed, units rejected and why
Retained sample
Number of packs kept and where stored
Release
Signature of the person who checked the batch before sale

Then keep a **distribution record**: date, buyer name and phone, batch number and quantity. A notebook works; a simple spreadsheet works better because you can search it. Keep retained samples from each batch until after its best-before date, so you can compare them with a complained-about pack.
Tracing one pack
Pack batch code
Batch manufacturing record
Raw material suppliers
Distribution record
Every buyer of that batch
One code on the pack opens the whole history of that batch.
How long to keep records

Keep each batch record, distribution record and retained sample at least until the batch's best-before date has passed, and keep the paper or digital records for longer, ideally for the life of your certificate, because an inspector may ask to see past batches. Store paper records in a dry box away from the production floor, and photograph each completed sheet into a dated phone folder as a backup. If water, termites or a lost phone destroy one copy, the other survives.
When a customer complains
Worked example: a complaint and a quiet recall
For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt makes chin-chin. A shop owner calls to say a customer found a pack that smells rancid. The pack code is CC-260312-02.
Ngozi logs the complaint: date, caller, shop, pack code, problem. She asks the shop to keep the pack.
She immediately stops selling CC-260312-02 and sets aside any unsold packs from it in her store.
She opens the retained sample of that batch. It also smells slightly off. The batch record shows the frying oil was from a new supplier, bought cheaper.
Her distribution record shows the batch was 120 packs: 40 to this shop, 50 to a supermarket, 30 sold directly on WhatsApp to 9 customers.
She calls both shops to remove the batch, replaces it with packs from batch CC-260314-01, and messages the 9 WhatsApp customers offering a replacement.
She returns to her previous oil supplier, records the cause and the action taken, and reports the issue to NAFDAC through its complaints line, as her approved product was affected.

Within two days every remaining pack from the batch is off the shelves, customers are looked after, and the cause is fixed. Without batch and distribution records, she would have had to pull every pack she had sold.
When it could hurt someone, act first

If a complaint suggests illness, a foreign object or an allergic reaction, stop sales of that batch at once, keep the evidence, encourage the affected person to see a health worker, and contact NAFDAC. Do not wait to be sure before you stop sales.
Training a worker on records: show, do, check
**Show:** fill one batch record yourself while the worker watches, explaining each line and why it matters.
**Do:** the worker fills the next batch record while you watch, and you correct gently on the spot.
**Check:** for the next five batches, the worker fills the record alone and you check and sign each one.
When five records in a row are complete and correct, check weekly instead, and keep the trained worker's name on your role sheet.
Explain the why, not only the how. A worker who understands that the batch code is what saves the business in a recall will not skip it on a busy Saturday.
A batch code such as product-date-number links every pack to its record.
Batch, distribution and complaint records together make a recall small and quick.
Keep retained samples until after the best-before date.
Stop sales of a batch first when safety is in doubt, then investigate.

Changes are part of growth, but they need care. If you change the formula, the premises, the label claims or add a product, contact NAFDAC (or SON) and ask what is required **before** the changed product goes on sale. Update your master formula, label artwork and compliance file at the same time, so the paperwork always matches the product.
Worked example: working out reminder dates

For example, Zainab in Kano collected her micro scale listing certificate on 10 February 2026. Her fumigation was done on 5 January 2026 and her pest control operator advised repeating it every six months.
Listing expiry: two years after 10 February 2026 is 10 February 2028.
Renewal reminder: six months before expiry is 10 August 2027. She enters it with an alarm.
Fumigation: six months after 5 January 2026 is 5 July 2026, then 5 January 2027, and so on. She sets a reminder one month before each, on 5 June and 5 December.
Compliance day: she sets a repeating event on the first Monday of every month.
Zainab's phone now warns her early for every date, so her renewal starts six months before stock would become illegal to sell.
When to move up to small scale
You need to list a sixth product, beyond the five allowed at micro scale.
Your production staff will go above the five-employee micro scale description.
Buyers want larger volumes than your single designated room can make safely.
You are ready to write SOPs and pay for water analysis and certificates of analysis.
Worked example: a two-product launch plan in 90 days
For example, Esi in Calabar makes whipped shea butter and black soap. She has a CAC certificate, a draft label and a spare room, but has not applied to NAFDAC. Today is 1 November.
Days 1 to 14 (by 14 November): write the master formula for both products, seal retained samples, fix the label using the field checklist.
Days 15 to 30 (by 30 November): screen the window, paint, set up handwashing, start the cleaning log, book fumigation and staff medical tests.
Days 31 to 45 (by 15 December): create the portal account, upload documents, pay through Remita against the payment advice, book the inspection for a production day in early January.
Days 46 to 90 (by 30 January): set up batch, distribution and complaint records, run her first inspection, answer any queries with proof, and contact two target shops with her buyer pack.
She puts the expected certificate date, about eighteen weeks after applying, plus two weeks of buffer, in her calendar, and plans her label print run for after that date.
Esi has a dated plan with four checkpoints, every task tied to something she learned in this course, and a realistic idea of when she can sell to shops legally.
Keep the plan where you see it

Put the 90-day plan on the production room wall next to the cleaning log, and tick tasks as you finish them. Review it on your monthly compliance day and move any slipped task to a new date rather than deleting it.

Your compliance file is now an asset. It holds your route decision, master formulas, labels, certificates, batch records and calendar. A bank, grant programme or large buyer who sees an organised file sees a producer they can trust.
Most lapses come from forgotten expiry dates, so put every date in a calendar with early reminders.

NAFDAC's scheme page names bread, packaged water, and kitchen-scale and micro-scale foods. On the cosmetic and household side, it lists shea butter, petroleum jelly, oils, soaps and laundry detergents, among others.

At micro scale, meat, milk and fish are excluded, except dried meat and dried fish, because germs grow in them quickly. Complex cosmetics, pressurised sprays and hand sanitisers do not qualify. Those go through regular registration.

The micro scale rules
Not more than five employees
A designated clean room
Not more than five products
Listing certificate valid for two years
A micro scale facility has not more than five employees.
It needs at least one designated room that does not open directly to a toilet, a refuse dump or an open gutter. The route depends on where you make the product, not only what it is.
Only five products can be registered. For example, Amaka makes seven, so she ranks them by monthly sales. Her top five are 680 of her 745 monthly units, about 91 percent. She pauses the other two.
The listing certificate is valid for two years. Mark the expiry date the day you collect it.

Lock the formula before you apply
The vetting sample must be exactly the product you will sell.
Weigh one normal batch
Turn weights into percentages
Write the method with times and heat
Make three batches; check they match
For example, Rukayat in Ilorin made whipped shea butter by feel. So she weighs one normal batch: 1,600 g shea butter, 300 g coconut oil, 80 g almond oil and 20 g fragrance oil. That is 2,000 g.
As percentages, that is 80 percent shea, 15 coconut, 4 almond and 1 fragrance. They add up to 100.
She writes the method: melt at low heat, cool until just setting, whip 8 minutes, and fill 10 jars of 200 g.
She makes three batches from the sheet, and all three come out the same.
If you change the recipe after approval, you are selling something that was never assessed.
Step four
Label fields, in English
Common product name and net weight
Batch number, manufacturing and best-before
Space reserved for the NAFDAC number
Storage, directions and allergy caution
Check every label field before you print the three labels. Write the common name, not just a brand, and net weight in metric units like 200 g. List all ingredients, largest first.
Add a batch number, dates, and your full address. Reserve a space for the NAFDAC number, and never print NAFDAC approved before approval.
Set best-before from your own sealed samples, checked every two weeks, and make it shorter than the last good check.
Safety first
Safety items that take time
Groundnut, sesame, wheat, egg, milk, almond: name them in ingredients and an allergy caution.
Pest control of the production premises by an operator. Keep the certificate.
Sputum, stool, urine, Widal and Hepatitis B tests for everyone who handles the food.
Allergens are a safety field. Groundnut, sesame, wheat, egg, milk and tree nut oils like almond can cause serious reactions. If any is in your product, even a little, name it clearly.
Arrange pest control of your production premises, and keep the fumigation certificate.
And book medical fitness tests early for everyone who will touch the product, because they take time.
Worked example
A tempting offer
For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes coconut candy, and a supermarket wants 200 packs a month.
Price per pack
Monthly sales at risk
Naira prices are approximate.

The supermarket needs a NAFDAC number. A man at the market offers to arrange one in seven days, for a fee. Funmi asks: will my room be inspected and my product tested? He says no. So it is not a genuine registration.
At about 1,500 naira a pack, 300,000 naira of monthly sales could be seized, plus the supermarket relationship.
So she applies on NAFDAC's portal with her own login, pays only against an official payment advice, and keeps the buyer updated. Never pay cash for the inspector.
Key points
Remember
Check your product type and your room
Micro scale: five staff, five products
Lock the formula as weights and percentages
Every label field, allergens included
No inspection and lab test? Not real
To remember. Check both your product type and your room. Micro scale means not more than five staff and five products. Lock your formula as weights and percentages.
Fill every label field, including allergens. And any offer that skips inspection and lab testing is not a real registration.

Business Registration & Compliance for Product Makers
Module 2 video
Apply, pass inspection, and price compliance into every pack
Apply, pass inspection, and price compliance into every pack.
This is the video for module two of Business Registration and Compliance: the application, the production room and the numbers.
Why this matters
Systems that carry you to approval
Six stages, about ninety working days
A room that passes hygiene checks
Compliance is a cost, like oil or packaging
NAFDAC's small business procedure has six stages, with a stated timeline of ninety working days. Doing each stage well stops your file from stalling.
The inspector checks good manufacturing and hygiene practice, so your room and habits must be ready.
And compliance is a real cost of production. If you do not build it into your price, it quietly eats your profit.
Step by step
From portal to certificate
Apply on the portal, details as on CAC
Pay through Remita using the advice only
Book inspection on a production day
Samples go to the laboratory
Answer queries with proof of each fix
Collect certificate; diary the expiry
Create your account on NAFDAC's portal with an email and phone you control. Enter your company details exactly as on your CAC certificate, because a different spelling causes queries.
Pay through Remita using the official payment advice only, and keep the receipt.
You can choose your inspection date. Pick a day you are producing, at least two weeks after fumigation, with medical certificates in hand.
Samples are collected and sent to the laboratory. Plan ahead: ninety working days is about 18 weeks. For example, Chiamaka adds 2 weeks of buffer and applies 20 weeks before her trade fair.
Treat every query as a task list. Fix it, keep proof, and reply through the official channel.
Collect your certificate, and diary the expiry with a reminder six months before. Only then add the number to your labels.
Production room
A designated room is used only for production, not a family kitchen. Contamination happens when dirty and clean things cross, so materials move one way.
For example, Grace in Jos converts a 3 by 4 metre room for chin-chin. Its back door faced the compound toilet, so she sealed it. Raw materials sit on a shelf by the front door.
Next comes the mixing table, then frying under a screened window.
Then the cooling rack, and the packing table in the far corner. Waste leaves by a route that does not pass the packing table.
She adds a handwashing point with soap, a pedal bin with a lid, and shelves 15 cm off the floor.
Inspection day
What the inspector looks at
Room: clean, screened, no opening to toilet
Water and soap for handwashing
Aprons, hair covers, medical certificates
Materials off the floor, labelled, receipts
Formula, batch records, cleaning log
Product from a normal batch for samples
Walk into your own room as if you were the inspector. Is it clean and screened? Is there water and soap for handwashing? Are workers in aprons and hair covers, with certificates on file?
Are materials off the floor and labelled? Are your formula, batch records, cleaning log and fumigation certificate ready in one show file? And is there product from a normal batch for samples?
Safety first
Outside or ventilated, away from frying, with a working regulator and hose.
Keep a fire blanket or extinguisher within reach.
Never mix bleach with other cleaners. Store chemicals apart from ingredients, labelled.
Keep gas cylinders outside or in a ventilated spot, away from the frying area, with a working regulator and hose.
Never mix bleach with other cleaners, because some combinations release harmful gas. Store cleaning chemicals on a separate shelf, in their original labelled containers.
And nobody works on production while sick with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
Worked example
Compliance cost per pack
For example, Grace sells about 300 packs of chin-chin a month, with a two-year listing.
First compliance costs
Repeat tests in year two
Two-year total
Per pack, over 7,200 packs
Other costs per pack
Fees can change. Quotes are illustrative.

Grace lists her compliance costs: the NAFDAC fee from her payment advice, medical tests, fumigation, label redesign and room improvements. Fees can change, so always confirm them, and get real quotes.
They add up to 206,737.50 naira. Repeating fumigation and medical tests in year two adds 70,000, making 276,737.50.
Over two years she sells 7,200 packs. Divided out, that is about 38.44 naira a pack, rounded up to 40.
With her other costs of 620 naira, each pack now costs 660. At 1,000 naira, she still makes 340 profit.
At only 50 packs a month, the same costs would be about 231 naira a pack. That is why you list your best sellers first.
Key points
Remember
Ninety working days is about 18 weeks
Inspect on a real production day
Designated room, one-way flow
Gas outside, never mix bleach
Spread compliance cost over units sold
To remember. Plan about 18 weeks plus a buffer. Book the inspection on a production day. Keep a designated room with one-way flow.
Keep gas away from heat and never mix bleach. And spread compliance cost over the units you sell.

Business Registration & Compliance for Product Makers
Module 3 video
Standards, batch records and staying approved
Standards, batch records, and staying approved.
This is the video for module three of Business Registration and Compliance: growth, traceability and renewals.
Why this matters
Approval is the start, not the finish
Some products need SON, not only NAFDAC
Trace any pack back to its batch
Handle a complaint without losing everything
Never let a certificate quietly expire
Approval is the start, not the finish. Makers of textiles, leather goods, candles or paving stones may need the Standards Organisation of Nigeria, SON, not NAFDAC.
As you grow, products travel to shops and homes you never see. Traceability means that from any one pack, you can find when it was made, from what, by whom, and where the rest of that batch went.
And most approved makers fall out of compliance not by fraud, but by forgetting a date.
SON MANCAP
The MANCAP steps
Ask SON before you spend, and keep the answer in writing.
Contact a SON state office or apply online
CAC certificate, lab test report, payment
At least two quarterly inspections
Certificate and logo with a unique number
Quarterly checks; recertify after three years
MANCAP is SON's certification scheme for locally made products, against Nigerian Industrial Standards.
For example, Bola in Abeokuta dyes adire, and a retail chain wants to stock it. She visits the SON state office and writes down the officer's name and answer.
She submits her CAC certificate, a test report from a SON or IPAN-accredited laboratory, and proof of payment.
SON inspects at least twice, a quarter apart, before certifying. So Bola expects at least six months, and asks about the fast track for small businesses.
She then receives the certificate and logo. It is valid for three years, with inspections every quarter, so her records must stay alive, not be prepared once.
Traceability
Code: product, date, batch of the day
Batch record: ingredients, suppliers, times
Distribution record: who got which batch
Retained samples kept past best-before
A batch is everything made from one mix. Give it a code and print it on every pack. For example, CC-260312-02 means chin-chin, made on 12 March 2026, second batch that day.
The batch record lists each ingredient, its supplier and expiry date, key times and temperatures, and who checked the batch.
A distribution record lists the date, buyer, batch and quantity. And keep retained samples from each batch until after the best-before date.
Worked example
A complaint and a quiet recall
If it could hurt someone, stop sales first. Then investigate.
Log the complaint and pack code
Stop selling that batch at once
Check retained sample and batch record
Find every buyer in the distribution record
Remove, replace, fix the cause, report
For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt gets a call. A pack of chin-chin smells rancid. She logs the complaint and the code, CC-260312-02, and asks the shop to keep the pack.
She stops selling that batch immediately.
Her retained sample also smells slightly off, and the batch record shows the frying oil came from a new, cheaper supplier.
Her distribution record shows 120 packs: 40 to this shop, 50 to a supermarket, and 30 sold on WhatsApp to 9 customers.
She removes and replaces the batch, contacts all 9 customers, goes back to her old oil supplier, and reports to NAFDAC. Within two days, it is done.
If a complaint suggests illness, a foreign object or an allergic reaction, stop sales at once, keep the evidence, encourage the person to see a health worker, and contact NAFDAC.
Training
Teach records: show, do, check
Fill one batch record yourself while the worker watches, explaining why each line matters.
The worker fills the next record while you watch, and you correct gently on the spot.
For the next five batches, the worker fills it alone and you check and sign each one.
Train workers in three steps. Show: fill one batch record yourself while they watch.
Do: they fill the next one while you watch and correct gently.
Check: for five batches, they fill it alone and you sign each one.
Explain the why. A worker who knows the batch code saves the business in a recall will not skip it on a busy Saturday.
Staying approved
Your compliance calendar
Listing certificate: remind 6 months before
MANCAP: each quarter, and before expiry
Fumigation: one month before due
Medical tests: at hiring and when due
Compliance review: first Monday monthly
For example, Zainab collected her listing certificate on 10 February 2026. It expires two years later, so she sets a renewal alarm for 10 August 2027, six months early.
She sets fumigation reminders a month before each due date, checks medical tests for every new worker, and reviews her file on the first Monday of every month.
Before changing a formula, pack, label claim, address or product, ask NAFDAC or SON first.
Key points
Remember
Ask SON whether your product needs MANCAP
Product-date-number codes on every pack
Batch and distribution records shrink recalls
When safety is in doubt, stop sales first
Every expiry date in a calendar, early
To remember. Ask SON whether your product needs MANCAP. Put a batch code on every pack. Batch and distribution records make a recall small and quick.
When safety is in doubt, stop sales first. And put every expiry date in a calendar with early reminders.
